activities.title: Embedded systems and IoT
activities.description: Ten questions on microcontrollers, sensors and actuators, analogue and digital signals, polling and interrupts, real-time constraints and the risks of connected devices — the ground covered by ALT 4. Written for Leaving Certificate Computer Science.

options.text: Any computer that is connected to the internet.
A general-purpose computer with the operating system installed on a chip.
A computer built into a larger device to carry out one dedicated job, such as the controller in a washing machine.
Software that is stored inside another program.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly separates sensors from actuators?

options.text: A motor is a sensor; a thermistor is an actuator.
A thermistor is a sensor; a motor is an actuator.
Both are sensors, because both are connected to the microcontroller.
Both are actuators, because both use electricity.

questions.stem: A microcontroller must read the voltage from a light sensor, which varies smoothly between 0 V and 3.3 V. What component does it need?

options.text: An analogue-to-digital converter, to turn the continuous voltage into a number.
A digital-to-analogue converter, to turn the number into a voltage.
A modem, to modulate the signal.
Nothing — a processor can read a voltage directly as a number.

questions.stem: An ADC has a resolution of 10 bits. How many distinct levels can it distinguish?
Why is a small microcontroller used in a central heating thermostat rather than a full desktop computer?

options.text: Desktop computers cannot read sensors.
Microcontrollers run programs faster than desktop processors.
It costs a fraction as much, uses very little power, fits in the case, and does everything the job requires.
A thermostat's software cannot be written for a desktop machine.

questions.stem: What is the difference between polling and using an interrupt to detect a button press?

options.text: Polling is done by the hardware; an interrupt is done in software.
Polling means the program repeatedly checks the button itself; an interrupt means the hardware signals the processor when the press happens.
They are two names for the same technique.
Polling is used for outputs and interrupts for inputs.

questions.stem: An airbag controller must fire within a few milliseconds of a crash being detected. What kind of requirement is this?

options.text: A real-time constraint — a correct result delivered late is a failure.
A bandwidth constraint.
A storage constraint.
A usability requirement.
The physical circuit board inside a device.
An app the user installs on a phone to control a device.
Data collected by a device's sensors.
The program held in a device's non-volatile memory that controls its hardware, updated rarely if at all.

questions.stem: What makes something an Internet of Things device rather than just an embedded system?

options.text: It has more than one sensor.
It is battery powered.
It is network-connected, so it can send its data and be controlled remotely.
It runs a full operating system.

questions.stem: A cheap internet-connected security camera ships with the same default password on every unit and no way to update its software. Why is that dangerous?

options.text: The camera will run out of storage.
Anyone can find the default password online and log in, and a flaw discovered later can never be patched — which is how thousands of such cameras have been recruited into botnets.
The video quality will degrade over time.
It will use too much electricity.

q1.explanation: An embedded system is dedicated to one function inside a larger product, and the user usually does not think of it as a computer at all. Most processors made each year go into embedded systems, not into laptops and phones. Internet connection is optional — that is what makes it IoT.

q2.explanation: A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal the system can read in; an actuator turns a signal into a physical effect out. Thermistor, LDR and microphone are inputs; motor, LED, buzzer and relay are outputs.

q3.explanation: The world is analogue and a processor works only in discrete numbers, so an ADC samples the voltage and reports a value. A DAC does the reverse — driving a speaker, say. This conversion is where quantisation error creeps in.

q4.explanation: n bits give 2^n levels: 2^10 = 1024, numbered 0 to 1023. Over a 0–3.3 V range that is a step of about 3.2 mV. 512 would be 9-bit resolution. More bits means finer measurement, at the cost of speed and price.

q5.explanation: Embedded design is about fitting the job: cost, power, size and reliability all matter more than raw speed, and a thermostat needs almost none of a desktop's capability. A microcontroller with no operating system also starts instantly and can run for years untouched.

q6.explanation: Polling burns processor time asking 'has it happened yet?' and can miss a short event between checks. An interrupt lets the processor do something else — or sleep, saving battery — until the hardware raises a signal that diverts it into a handler.

q7.explanation: In a hard real-time system the deadline is part of correctness: an airbag that fires 200 ms late is as bad as one that does not fire. This is why such systems avoid anything with unpredictable timing, including general-purpose operating systems.

q8.explanation: Firmware sits between hardware and software: it is a program, but it lives in the device and is rarely changed. That is exactly why a device with no update mechanism is a long-term security problem — see the last question.

q9.explanation: IoT is an embedded system plus a network connection. That connection is what makes remote monitoring possible, and it is also what turns a private device into something reachable by anyone on the internet if it is not secured.

q10.explanation: Shared default credentials mean one published password unlocks every unit, and with no update path a vulnerability is permanent. The Mirai botnet of 2016 was built almost entirely from such devices, and used them to knock large parts of the internet offline.
